A home Wi-Fi network works by using a router and an access point to connect devices. The router acts as the central hub, directing all the devices to connect to it. The access point, which is usually a wireless router, is connected to the router and is responsible for directing all the devices to connect to it.

When a device wants to connect to the internet, it sends a request to the router. The router then forwards the request to the access point. The access point then forwards the request to the wireless router, which in turn forwards it to the internet.

The packets of data that are sent from the internet to the access point are called packets. These packets are sent in the form of data streams, which are then transmitted over the radio channels. The radio channels are the physical paths that the packets take to reach their destination.

When two devices transmit at once, they are essentially sending the same packet. The packets are then combined and retransmitted to ensure that they reach their destination without any loss. This process is called multiplexing.
